== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concern (cross-sectional exclusions and missingness): Longitudinal attrition is not applicable to repeated cross-sectional surveys, but household survey response/refusal rates were not reported, 29.8% (544/1,825 in 2016) and 29.2% (561/1,921 in 2017) of completed surveys were excluded post-hoc because households had no child under 5 years, and FCR measurements were missing for 74/1,281 (5.8%) analytic households in 2016 and 16/1,360 (1.2%) in 2017 without sensitivity analysis.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Community Water Safety Plan (WSP) programming and water supply types were non-randomly distributed (e.g., 0% WSP coverage in Quneitra vs. 46.7%–50.5% in Dar'a). Although multivariable and sub-district mixed-effects regressions were run, covariate control relied on univariable and forward-stepwise p-value screening, omitted measured demographic confounders (household size, head age, female headship, number of children <5), and could not adjust for unmeasured security, power-supply, or infrastructure differences in cross-sectional data.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / indirect operationalization: Although the paper discusses UN Security Council Resolution 2165, the Whole of Syria WASH coordination architecture, private water-trucking markets, and regulatory governance via Water Safety Plans (WSPs), empirical measurement of institutional/regulatory exposure is limited to an unverified binary indicator of whether a household lived in a WSP-targeted community and self-reported reliance on piped network versus private trucked water, with no direct measurement of legal rules, vendor regulation, or household-level intervention fidelity.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (mixed across measures): Household free chlorine residual (FCR) and pH were measured objectively with a Lovibond Colorimeter and DPD-1/phenol red reagents, and soap/water at handwashing stations was directly observed, but childhood diarrhea relied on 2-week caregiver recall with no standard definition of diarrhea provided, toilet functionality in regressions relied on self-report rather than enumerator observation, and the hygiene item question conflated market availability with household affordability.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Mixed (adequate objective proxy for water chlorination; weak for diarrheal health outcome): Drinking water residual chlorination (FCR > 0.1 mg/L) was measured objectively at the household using a Lovibond Colorimeter and DPD-1 tablets (though microbiological parameters were not tested), whereas childhood diarrhea (<5 years in the past 2 weeks) was measured via unvalidated caregiver self-report without providing a standard case definition.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern / Can't tell on pre-registration: No pre-specified study protocol or analysis plan is cited (secondary IRB approval only), 2016 FCR regressions were omitted due to low FCR prevalence, forward stepwise p-value filtering selectively determined reported multivariable estimates, and text descriptions of Table 6 inconsistently labeled odds ratios <1 and >1 as protective or risk factors.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: The sampling frame was restricted to opposition-controlled areas of Dar'a and Quneitra where safe access was possible (with active-conflict communities deferred), within-community household sampling procedures varied across communities (map neighborhood division vs. random routes), non-response rates were unreported, and ~30% of surveyed households without children <5 were excluded post-hoc even for household water quality analyses.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The target sampling frame and analytic inclusion criteria were explicitly stated: permanent resident and IDP households in safely accessible opposition-controlled communities across 17 sub-districts of Dar'a and Quneitra governorates, followed by an explicit analytic restriction excluding households without children under five years of age (yielding n=1,281 in 2016 and n=1,360 in 2017).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2–4 (Methods; Statistical analysis; Results - Household survey)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The conflict context, geographic setting (17 sub-districts comprising 50 communities in Dar'a and 14 in Quneitra, mapped in Fig. 1), survey timing (June/July 2016 and February 2017), and household demographic and WASH characteristics (household size, IDP share, female-headed households, head age, shelter damage, water sources, and sanitation) are described in detail in Tables 1 and 2.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2–8 (Methods; Fig. 1; Results; Tables 1 and 2)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposures were derived from a 24-question ODK survey with mixed validity: handwashing soap/water was directly observed, whereas WSP exposure was coded solely as a community-level binary indicator without verifying household-level exposure, FunctionalToilet in regressions relied on self-report despite substantial divergence from observed clean/functional toilets (95.1%–96.8% vs. 63.8%–69.5%), and the authors explicitly note that HygieneAccess failed to distinguish between market availability and affordability.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3–5, 8–9, 12 (Household survey; Tables 1–3; Discussion limitations)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: While household water chlorination status was assessed using objective colorimetric criteria (FCR > 0.1 mg/L via Lovibond Colorimeter and DPD-1 tablets), the diarrheal health condition in children <5 lacked objective or standard clinical/epidemiological criteria; the authors explicitly state in Limitations that self-reported diarrhea is subject to response bias and no standard definition of diarrhea was provided to respondents.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3, 11 (Water quality testing; Discussion limitations)

domain_ratings.justification: Potential confounding variables including internal displacement status (Displacement), shelter damage (Shelter), share of income spent on water (IncomeSpent), co-occurring WASH conditions, and sub-district clustering were identified and included among candidate regression variables, although measured demographic factors (household size, head age, female headship, number of children <5) and community security/electricity differences were omitted from regression tables.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors stated and implemented multivariable logistic regression and sub-district mixed-effects logistic regression to adjust for co-occurring covariates and geographic clustering by sub-district, although adjustment quality was weakened by univariate/forward-stepwise p-value screening and complete non-overlap of WSP programming in Quneitra (0%).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcome validity differed sharply between the two co-primary outcomes: household free chlorine residual (FCR > 0.1 mg/L) was validly and objectively measured by trained enumerators using a Lovibond Colorimeter and DPD-1 tablets (though without microbiological testing), whereas two-week childhood diarrhea was measured by unvalidated caregiver recall with no standard definition of diarrhea provided to respondents.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3, 11 (Household survey; Water quality testing; Discussion limitations)

domain_ratings.justification: Several statistical flaws undermine the analysis: (1) ~30% of surveyed households (those without children <5) were excluded post-hoc even from household water FCR analyses, for which sample size was not powered; (2) unadjusted two-sample t-tests were used to compare clustered binary proportions between 2016 and 2017 (Table 2); (3) forward-stepwise variable selection based on univariable significance screening was used; (4) both continuous FCR and dichotomized FCR_Bin were entered simultaneously into the 2017 multivariable diarrhea model (Table 5), introducing collinearity; and (5) text interpretations of Table 6 inconsistently inverted protective versus risk directions for odds ratios.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3, 7–11 (Statistical analysis; Results; Tables 2, 5, 6; Discussion limitations)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Sikder et al. (2018) report secondary analyses of two repeated cross-sectional household WASH surveys conducted in June/July 2016 (n=1,281 households with children <5 analyzed out of 1,825 surveyed) and February 2017 (n=1,360 analyzed out of 1,921 surveyed) across 17 sub-districts in opposition-controlled Dar'a and Quneitra governorates, southern Syria. Because each round was analyzed cross-sectionally via multivariable and sub-district mixed-effects logistic regressions without a quasi-experimental comparator structure (no panel tracking, DiD, IV, RDD, or matched control design), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the appropriate appraisal instrument. Notable strengths in an active conflict environment include probability-proportionate-to-size community sampling across 64 communities, direct household colorimetric testing of free chlorine residual (FCR) and pH, direct observation of handwashing stations, and sub-district random effects. However, overall methodological concern is High: sampling was restricted to safely accessible opposition-held areas with variable within-community household selection and ~30% post-hoc exclusion of households without children <5; caregiver-reported childhood diarrhea lacked any standard case definition; hygiene item access conflated market availability with affordability; community WSP programming was non-randomly concentrated entirely in Dar'a (0% in Quneitra); and statistical modeling relied on forward stepwise p-value screening, unclustered two-sample t-tests on binary proportions, and simultaneous inclusion of collinear continuous and binary FCR variables in Table 5.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Repeated analytical cross-sectional household surveys (2016 and 2017 rounds analyzed via descriptive comparisons and separate cross-sectional multivariable and mixed-effects logistic regressions)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Methods: sampling, household survey, water quality testing, and statistical analysis (PDF Pages 2–3); Results and Tables 1–6 (PDF Pages 3–10); Discussion and study limitations (PDF Pages 10–12).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes two cross-sectional household survey rounds (2016 and 2017) using cross-sectional multivariable and mixed-effects logistic regressions within each survey year to examine associations between 15 demographic/WASH variables and household water FCR > 0.1 mg/L or caregiver-reported childhood diarrhea. As the authors explicitly note on PDF Page 11, the data come from cross-sectional surveys rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental intervention design (no DiD, ITS, RDD, IV, PSM, or longitudinal cohort follow-up), making the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies the exact matching tool.
